John L. Girardeau
JON JEE-rar-doh
proper noun
The given name John from the Hebrew Yōhānān, “the LORD is gracious”; the surname Girardeau, of French Huguenot origin, a diminutive of Gérard, “brave with the spear.”

Biblical Definition

John Lafayette Girardeau (1825–1898), of Huguenot descent and Southern Presbyterian conviction, is remembered as a preacher of extraordinary power who gave the strength of his early ministry to the gospel among the enslaved of Charleston. At the Zion Church he gathered a great congregation of black worshippers, labouring among them with such fervour and such evident love that revival attended his preaching, and multitudes professed faith in Christ. He held that the gospel is for every soul without distinction, and that the Redeemer purchased worshippers out of every people; and he counted it no small part of his calling to bring the riches of Reformed truth to the poor and the bond. Afterward he became professor of theology at Columbia Seminary, where his lectures upon the doctrines of grace, the work of the Spirit, and the freedom of the will defended the old Calvinism against Arminian and rationalist error. A man of deep piety and mighty in prayer, Girardeau joined the passion of an evangelist to the precision of a theologian. His life witnesses that sovereign grace stoops to the lowliest, that the gospel levels every earthly rank before the cross, and that the same Spirit who quickens the mighty quickens the humble. He teaches the church to preach Christ freely to all, honouring in every hearer a soul for whom the Saviour shed His precious blood.

Webster 1828 Definition

Southern Presbyterian who preached to the enslaved of Charleston and taught the doctrines of grace.

A Presbyterian minister (1825–1898) of Huguenot descent, of powerful evangelistic gifts.

The pastor of Zion Church in Charleston, where he preached to a great congregation of the enslaved.

A preacher under whom revival attended, with multitudes professing faith in Christ.

Afterward professor of theology at Columbia Seminary, defending the old Calvinism.

A man mighty in prayer who joined the evangelist’s passion to the theologian’s precision.

Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle that sovereign grace stoops to the lowliest.

expand to see more

This entry is preserved to honour a preacher whose labours proved that the gospel levels every earthly rank before the cross. Girardeau carried the riches of Reformed truth to the poor and the bond, and revival attended a ministry that owned in every hearer a soul for whom Christ died.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the freeness of the gospel to every soul without distinction, and the stooping of sovereign grace to the humble and the weak. Where our age would either despise the lowly or reduce the gospel to a merely social remedy, Girardeau calls the church to preach Christ crucified to all, honouring each hearer as one for whom the Redeemer shed His precious blood.

Hebrew Roots

The name joins “the LORD is gracious” to a French Huguenot surname.

expand to see more

John comes from the Hebrew Yōhānān, “the LORD is gracious.”

Girardeau is a French Huguenot surname, a diminutive of Gérard, “brave with the spear.”

The name reflects the Huguenot exiles who carried Reformed faith to the American South.

It became bound to Zion Church in Charleston and to Columbia Seminary.

In church history “Girardeau” stands for sovereign grace preached freely to the lowly.

Usage

"Girardeau’s Charleston ministry brought Reformed truth to the enslaved."

"As a Columbia professor, John L. Girardeau defended the doctrines of grace."

"Like Girardeau, faithful preachers own in every hearer a soul for whom Christ died."
